title: Effect of Sintering Temperature on the Microstructure and Integrated Properties of MgAlTiVFeCo Lightweight High-Entropy Alloy

recollection.starting_material: A mixture of elemental powders of Magnesium (Mg), Aluminum (Al), Titanium (Ti), Vanadium (V), Iron (Fe), and Cobalt (Co) in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios.
recollection.intervention: The powder mixture was consolidated via spark plasma sintering (SPS) or hot pressing at various temperatures (e.g., 800°C to 1200°C) to form a bulk alloy, followed by microstructural characterization and mechanical testing.
recollection.structure: A dual-phase microstructure consisting of a primary Mg-based solid solution matrix and secondary intermetallic phases (likely BCC or HCP structures containing Fe, Co, and Ti), with grain size increasing as sintering temperature rises.
recollection.mechanism: Higher sintering temperatures promoted atomic diffusion and grain growth, leading to the dissolution of some metastable phases and the coarsening of precipitates, which altered the balance between strength and ductility.
recollection.results: The study likely found an optimal sintering temperature (e.g., 1000°C) that maximized the combination of density (approx. 4.5 g/cm³), yield strength (approx. 400-500 MPa), and ductility (approx. 10-15% elongation), while lower temperatures resulted in incomplete densification and higher temperatures led to excessive grain coarsening and reduced strength.

score.note: The recollection correctly identifies SPS and the optimal 1000 °C condition, despite hedging with hot pressing. Its proposed Mg-based dual-phase structure and grain-coarsening mechanism do not match the dense microstructure with uniformly distributed oxide barrier phases or the reported passivation, chloride-blocking, and diffusion-controlled oxidation mechanisms. The density, strength, and ductility estimates are unrelated to the reported 96.7% density, 1235.5 HV hardness, oxidation constants, and electrochemical values.
